name: Tesofensine

lead: Tesofensine is an oral drug promoted for strong appetite suppression and fat loss, and some users see it as an alternative to approved weight-loss drugs. It was first tested for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, then pursued for obesity after trial participants lost weight.

It blocks the reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in the brain; in animals this reduces appetite through hypothalamic circuits. In a 24-week phase II trial in 203 obese adults published in The Lancet in 2008, placebo-adjusted weight loss ranged from about 4.5% to 10.6% across the three doses tested.

paras: It is a daily oral drug. Later work combined it with metoprolol (Tesomet) for rare forms of obesity. On looksmax.org it is discussed as a weight-loss option that users source outside regulated channels.

Reported effects include dry mouth, nausea, insomnia and increases in heart rate and blood pressure. Related drugs such as sibutramine were withdrawn for safety reasons. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA, and supply outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: Tesofensine is promoted for strong appetite suppression and fat loss. It blocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, so you eat less and carry less body fat. A 24-week trial found weight loss beyond placebo of about 4.5 to 10.6 percent, with raised heart rate and blood pressure; it is not approved.

lead: Tesofensine (development code NS2330) is an investigational oral drug that blocks the reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. For people interested in how they look, the draw is appetite suppression: in clinical trials participants ate less and lost weight and body fat beyond what diet alone produced, which is the route by which fat-loss and leaner-physique communities discuss it [1][2][3].

It was developed by the Danish company NeuroSearch, first for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and then pursued as an obesity treatment after weight loss was observed in those trials [2][4]. A 24-week phase II trial in 203 obese adults, published in The Lancet in 2008, found weight loss of 4.5%, 9.2% and 10.6% at the three doses tested against 2.0% with diet plus placebo [1][5]. Later work combined it with the beta-blocker metoprolol (Tesomet) in rare forms of obesity [6]. Development rights passed from NeuroSearch to Saniona in 2014, and a licensee has pursued approval in Mexico [3][7]. It is not approved by the US FDA or the European Medicines Agency for any use [8][9].

Reported adverse effects in the literature include dry mouth, nausea, constipation, insomnia and increases in heart rate, with blood pressure effects varying across trials and doses [1][4][7]. It is discussed on looksmax.org and in fitness communities as a weight-loss option that users source outside regulated channels [10][7].

paras: No major regulator has approved tesofensine. Its studied use is obesity, including hypothalamic obesity and Prader-Willi syndrome, usually in combination with metoprolol as Tesomet [6][11][12]. The first obesity trials treated otherwise healthy adults with obesity who followed a modest calorie-restricted diet [1].

Interest in appearance centres on fat loss and appetite suppression: eating less leads to a lower body weight and body fat, and a leaner look. In the TIPO-1 trial, weight loss with tesofensine exceeded diet plus placebo at every dose [1]. Grokipedia notes attention from bodybuilding and fitness communities during cutting phases, and a looksmax.org thread has users asking each other about experiences with the drug [7][10].

Phase II trials in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, which began in 2003, did not lead to approval for those conditions, but weight loss occurred in participants [2][4][13][14][15]. A pooled analysis of four 14-week trials in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's patients (740 on tesofensine, 228 on placebo) reported dose-dependent weight loss of up to 2.8% in the whole cohort and 3.7% in the obese subgroup at the highest dose, about 4% placebo-subtracted, with heart rate up by roughly 2 to 7 beats per minute and no effect on blood pressure [4].

The dedicated obesity trial, TIPO-1, ran at five Danish centres. After a two-week run-in, 203 adults with a BMI of 30 to 40 were randomised to once-daily tesofensine at three doses or placebo for 24 weeks, all on an energy-restricted diet. Mean weight loss was 2.0% for placebo and 4.5%, 9.2% and 10.6% for the three doses (all p<0.0001 versus placebo). Common side effects were dry mouth, nausea, constipation, diarrhoea and insomnia, and 79% completed the trial. Heart rate rose by 7.4 beats per minute over placebo in the middle-dose group and blood pressure did not rise significantly at the two lower doses [1][5]. The authors compared the result with the roughly 3 to 5 kg beyond placebo usually seen with approved drugs and called for phase III trials [1]. A 2009 review summarised the phase II findings as dose-related decreases in body weight, body fat and waist size [2].

A two-part appetite analysis (158 participants in the randomised part) found a dose-dependent rise in satiety around week 12 that correlated with weight loss; satiety scores fell back by week 24 and returned to baseline after the drug was withdrawn, and rose again when it was restarted, and the authors could not say whether the smaller late effect reflected the body's counter-response to lower weight or a waning of the drug's effect [16]. In a single-dose crossover study of 52 recreational stimulant users, tesofensine did not differ significantly from placebo on subjective measures, while amphetamine did, and the authors concluded its abuse potential was no greater than that of bupropion and atomoxetine [17]. Longer-term safety and energy-balance studies were registered [18][19].

A 24-week randomised trial of Tesomet (tesofensine with metoprolol) in 21 adults with hypothalamic obesity, published in 2022, reported about 6.3% additional weight loss over placebo, with 8 of 13 on Tesomet reaching at least 5% loss against 1 of 8 on placebo. Common events were sleep disturbance, dry mouth and headache, and one participant on Tesomet stopped after worsening of pre-existing anxiety [6]. Smaller registered phase II studies covered type 2 diabetes, Prader-Willi syndrome and hypothalamic injury [20][11][12]. A trial of about 372 patients is reported to have been run in Mexico by a licensee and to have reported in 2018 [7]. Animal studies report appetite suppression via noradrenergic and dopaminergic pathways and silencing of hypothalamic GABA neurons [21][22].

Trials report dry mouth, nausea, constipation, headache, diarrhoea and insomnia, with dry mouth and insomnia rising with dose. Wikipedia reports discontinuation due to adverse events of 13% on tesofensine versus 6% on placebo, and heart-rate rises of up to about 8 beats per minute at therapeutic doses with small blood pressure rises [3]. Reviewers cite cardiovascular safety as a concern for the class [2][23].

Reviews of centrally acting weight-loss drugs highlight that agents acting on monoamines can have neuropsychiatric effects and that earlier drugs in this space, such as sibutramine and rimonabant, were withdrawn for safety reasons [23][24]. In the hypothalamic obesity trial, one Tesomet participant discontinued after worsening anxiety [6]. Grokipedia also reports interaction concerns with MAO inhibitors and CYP3A4 inhibitors and rebound weight gain after stopping in some extension participants [7].

In vitro it potently blocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in synapses [2]. Wikipedia reports revised binding data placing the strongest effect at the noradrenaline transporter, then serotonin, then dopamine, and suggests this may relate to the weak Parkinson's results and to stimulant users not self-administering it reliably [3]. Rat studies point to indirect activation of alpha-1 adrenoceptor and dopamine D1 pathways as the basis of appetite suppression, and blocking alpha-1 receptors nearly abolished the effect [21]. A 2024 mouse and rat study reports silencing of lateral-hypothalamic GABAergic neurons, little repetitive head-weaving compared with phentermine at therapeutic doses, and no sign that the effect came from taste aversion [22].

Tesofensine is taken orally with roughly 90% bioavailability and has a long half-life of about 220 hours. It is mainly metabolised by CYP3A4 to a metabolite, NS2360, with a half-life of about 374 hours and a small share of the parent drug's activity; renal clearance accounts for only about 15 to 20% of elimination [3].

NeuroSearch developed the compound with Boehringer Ingelheim initially for neurodegenerative disease, and weight loss seen in patients led it to pursue obesity [2]. Rat studies on a high-fat diet supported the weight-reducing effect, and a 2009 review noted that the FDA had approved a phase III trial programme [2]. Development for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's ended around 2008 [7][3]. NeuroSearch transferred the rights to Saniona in 2014, according to Wikipedia, which cites a company announcement dated 30 October 2014 [3].

Grokipedia reports that Saniona licensed exclusive obesity rights for Mexico and Argentina to Productos Medix in 2016, that Medix filed for approval with Mexico's regulator COFEPRIS in 2019, that a favourable non-binding opinion followed in 2023, that approval was withheld in late 2024 pending more data and that Medix resubmitted in 2025; that source is AI-generated and some of its figures are inconsistent, so these details are reported as unconfirmed [7].

Tesofensine is not an authorised medicine in the US or EU and is listed in the US as an Investigational New Drug [3]. Forum users who discuss it describe obtaining it outside regulated supply [10][7]. Grokipedia describes Reddit discussion in some bodybuilding communities of tesofensine as an appetite suppressant for cutting, with users comparing it to GLP-1 drugs, and notes that these accounts are anecdotal [7]. Specific sourcing and dosing details are not provided here.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, tesofensine appears as a niche, non-prescription fat-loss option that members ask each other about; Grokipedia also describes it in cutting-phase discussions in fitness communities [10][7].
